package_info.why_malicious: The vulnerabilities CVE-2022-41040 (Server-Side Request Forgery) and CVE-2022-41082 (Remote Code Execution) allow remote attackers with authenticated access to chain exploits and achieve remote code execution via PowerShell, enabling full compromise of the Exchange server. Attackers can abuse the autodiscover endpoint to pivot into internal backend services and ultimately execute arbitrary commands.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, an authenticated user sends a specially crafted HTTP GET request to the autodiscover/autodiscover.json endpoint, abusing SSRF to force the Exchange server to access internal backend endpoints, which enables the attacker to pivot to further exploitation steps.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The request is intentionally crafted to exploit SSRF by embedding backend endpoint references and using the '@' character in the query, which is not part of any legitimate autodiscover workflow.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Exchange autodiscover requests do not contain embedded backend endpoint references, '@' symbols in the query, or attempt to access internal services via SSRF.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Autodiscover endpoints are used by email clients for configuration discovery, but never with parameters that reference internal backend endpoints or use '@' in this context.
key_indicators: autodiscover.json requests with embedded backend endpoint references
Presence of '@' in query parameters targeting autodiscover endpoint
Unusual or malformed Email parameter values
SSRF attempts to internal Exchange backend services

execution_context.file_location: PowerShell handler (Exchange backend, invoked via SSRF)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Remote PowerShell command execution via crafted HTTP request (details not shown in report, but implied by CVE-2022-41082 exploitation chain)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After successful SSRF exploitation, the attacker uses the backend PowerShell handler to execute arbitrary PowerShell commands remotely via HTTP requests, resulting in remote code execution and full compromise of the Exchange server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remote PowerShell execution triggered by user-controlled HTTP requests is only possible due to exploitation of chained vulnerabilities and is never a part of normal Exchange operation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Exchange should not allow arbitrary PowerShell code execution from user-controlled HTTP requests, especially those originating from SSRF chains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Exchange administrators may use PowerShell for legitimate management, but never via user-supplied HTTP requests or SSRF chains.
key_indicators: PowerShell execution initiated by HTTP requests
Chained exploitation from SSRF to backend management interface
Abuse of Exchange's PowerShell handler for arbitrary command execution

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted GET request to the autodiscover.json endpoint, exploiting SSRF (CVE-2022-41040).
attack_chain.leads_to: Access to internal Exchange backend endpoints.

attack_chain.action: Attacker leverages SSRF to access the PowerShell handler and executes arbitrary PowerShell commands (CVE-2022-41082).
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution and full compromise of the Exchange server.

behavioral_signatures: autodiscover.json HTTP requests with embedded backend endpoint references or '@' in query parameters
Authenticated HTTP requests containing unusual or malformed Email parameters targeting autodiscover endpoint
Remote PowerShell command execution initiated via HTTP requests, especially following suspicious autodiscover activity
file_indicators: No specific file indicators; detection should focus on Exchange HTTP request logs and PowerShell execution logs
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Exchange server HTTP logs for autodiscover.json requests containing unusual parameters, such as embedded backend endpoint references, '@' symbols, or malformed Email values. Correlate these with PowerShell execution logs to identify remote code execution triggered by HTTP requests. Alert on outbound connections to known malicious IPs or domains associated with Exchange exploitation. Automated detection should flag any sequence where an autodiscover SSRF is followed by backend PowerShell activity.
